procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of acquittal of Lala Ram, dated August 31, 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Hari Ram filed an application under s. 417(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code for leave to appeal against the Magistrate's order. The High Court granted leave and accepted the appeal, convicting Lala Ram under s. 324, I.P.C., and sentencing him to four months' rigorous imprisonment. Subsequently, an application was filed under s. 561-A, Cr. P.C., read with ss. 3, 4 and 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, but the High Court did not accede to this application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Lala Ram, the appellant, obtained special leave from the Supreme Court to appeal the High Court's judgment and order dated March 14, 1967, in Criminal Appeal No. 720 of 1965.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code prescribes a period of limitation, thereby making Section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act (which allows for the deduction of time taken to obtain a certified copy) applicable to an application for leave to appeal under Section 417(3).

facts: An application for leave to appeal a Magistrate's acquittal order was filed under Section 417(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC).
The application was filed after the 60-day period mentioned in Section 417(4) CrPC.
The applicant claimed the application was timely because two days required to obtain a certified copy of the order should be deducted, as per Section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act.
The appellant argued that the 60-day period in Section 417(4) is not a period of limitation, but a jurisdictional bar, and therefore Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act does not apply.
law: Section 417(4) of the CrPC states that no application for special leave to appeal an acquittal shall be 'entertained' by the High Court after sixty days from the date of the acquittal order.

Section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act allows for the time taken to obtain a certified copy of a court order to be excluded when computing the period of limitation for an appeal or an application for leave to appeal.
Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act provides that sections of the Limitation Act (like Section 12) apply to periods of limitation prescribed by any 'special law', unless expressly excluded.
application: The Supreme Court held that Section 417(4) of the CrPC itself prescribes a period of limitation. It reasoned that the legislature is free to prescribe a limitation period within a specific statute like the CrPC, rather than amending the Limitation Act.

The Court relied on its previous decision in *Kaushalya Rani v. Gopal Singh*, which had already characterized the 60-day period in Section 417(4) as a "period of limitation" and a "special law" of limitation.

By classifying Section 417(4) as a 'special law' that prescribes a period of limitation, the Court found that the provisions of the Limitation Act, specifically Section 12(2), would apply due to the operation of Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act.

The Court rejected the appellant's argument that Section 417(4) was a jurisdictional bar. It also clarified that the word "entertain" in the section means the filing or receipt of the application by the court, not the actual hearing of the matter.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that Section 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code prescribes a period of limitation. Consequently, Section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act is applicable, and the time taken to obtain a certified copy of the acquittal order must be deducted when calculating the 60-day period. Therefore, the application for leave to appeal was filed within the time limit.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the finding of fact arrived at by the High Court regarding the evidence of the eye-witnesses.

facts: The appellant's counsel argued that the High Court should not have interfered with the Magistrate's order of acquittal.
To support this, the counsel presented the evidence of two eyewitnesses to the Supreme Court: Poonaram, who was injured, and P.W. 3, Ananda, an independent witness.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence of the two eyewitnesses, Poonaram and Ananda.
After its review, the Supreme Court explicitly stated its agreement with the High Court's assessment.
The Court found that the High Court was correct in its view that the Magistrate was not entitled to reject the evidence of these eyewitnesses.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided not to interfere with the High Court's finding of fact because the appellant's counsel failed to provide any reason for the Court to do so.

issue.issue_text: Whether the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act should be extended to the appellant.

facts: After the High Court delivered its judgment, the appellant filed an application claiming he was 20 years old at the time of the offense.
The appellant argued that because of his age, he should have been given the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act.
The High Court rejected this application.
law: To receive the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, an individual must prove they were under the age of 21 at the relevant time.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the appellant was given an opportunity to prove his age.
However, the appellant failed to furnish any "good proof" to establish that he was under 21 years old at the time of the offense.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's request for the benefit of the Act because he failed to provide sufficient proof of his age, which was a necessary condition for eligibility.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code prescribes a period of limitation, thereby making Section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act (which allows for the deduction of time taken to obtain a certified copy) applicable to an application for leave to appeal under Section 417(3).
appellant_arguments: Section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act, which allows for deducting time to get a certified copy, is not applicable to applications for leave to appeal under Section 417(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
Section 417(4) is a prohibition that bars the High Court's jurisdiction to deal with the application if 60 days have passed since the acquittal order.
The word 'entertain' in Section 417(4) means 'to deal with or hear' the application, not just to file or receive it. Therefore, the hearing itself must be within 60 days.
respondent_arguments: The application for leave to appeal was filed within time because the two days required to obtain a certified copy of the Magistrate's order should be deducted from the total period, as per Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act.
The word 'entertain' in Section 417(4) means 'to file or be received by the Court' and does not refer to the actual hearing of the application.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the finding of fact arrived at by the High Court regarding the evidence of the eye-witnesses.
appellant_arguments: The High Court should not have interfered with the Magistrate's order of acquittal.
No offence was committed because the accused had a right of private defence of property.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was correct in its finding of fact and in overturning the acquittal, as the Magistrate was not entitled to reject the evidence of the eyewitnesses.
Even if a right of private defence existed, the appellant had ample opportunity to contact the authorities and should not have taken the law into his own hands.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act should be extended to the appellant.
appellant_arguments: The appellant was 20 years old at the time of the application and should have been given the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments are not detailed in the provided text, but their position would be to oppose the application, supporting the High Court's decision not to grant this benefit.

cases.principle: The rule of the 60-day bar for an application under s. 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code is a 'special law' of limitation within the meaning of s. 29(2) of the Limitation Act.
Section 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code itself prescribes a period of limitation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The right of private defense of property is not available when there is ample opportunity to have recourse to public authorities. The 60-day limitation period for an application under s.417(3) of the Code is a special law of limitation provided for within the Code itself.
obiter: An appellate court should not interfere with a finding of fact arrived at by a lower court unless a specific reason is shown.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that the 60-day period mentioned in Section 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code is a special rule of limitation, not a jurisdictional bar. Consequently, Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act applies, allowing for the deduction of time taken to obtain a certified copy of the acquittal order. The word "entertain" in this context means the filing or receipt of the application by the court, not its actual hearing, thus an application filed within the prescribed period, after deducting the necessary time, is considered to be within time.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory interpretation of the word 'entertain' within the context of Section 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
Application of precedent (Kaushalya Rani v. Gopal Singh) to determine if a statutory time limit constitutes a 'special law' of limitation.
Standard of appellate review for findings of fact, requiring a reason to be shown for the Supreme Court to interfere with a High Court's finding.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's interpretation that the word 'entertain' in s.417(4) means 'to deal with or hear', stating that in this context, it means 'file or received by the Court'.

The court, relying on its previous judgment in Kaushalya Rani v. Gopal Singh, held that the 60-day bar is a 'special law, that is to say, a rule of limitation which is specially provided for in the Code itself,' which makes other provisions of the Limitation Act applicable.
No reason was shown to the court why it should interfere with the finding of fact arrived at by the High Court regarding the evidence of the eye-witnesses.

The court dismissed the claim of a right of private defence by reasoning that even assuming such a right existed, the appellant 'had ample opportunity of· having recourse to the authorities and there was no need for the appellant to have taken the law into his own hands.'

The appellant failed to receive the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act because 'no good proof has been furnished to establish that the appellant was at the relevant time under the age of 21 years.'
why_respondent_won: The court agreed with the respondent's interpretation that 'entertain' means 'file or receive by the court and it has no reference to the actual hearing of the application for leave to appeal'.

The court's finding that Section 417(4) prescribes a period of limitation meant that the respondent was correct in arguing that the time taken to obtain a certified copy could be deducted, making the application timely.

The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's assessment that 'the Magistrate was not entitled to reject the evidence of the eye-witnessess' and found no reason to interfere with this finding of fact.
policy_considerations: Interpreting 'entertain' to mean the actual hearing of an application would lead to an unjust result where 'in many cases applications for leave to appeal would be barred because the applications have not been put up for hearing before the High Court within sixty days of the order of acquittal,' which is a consequence the court sought to avoid.
